a: in Seir
p: The Hebrew says Israel was crushed "in Seir." The Greek, Syriac and Latin read "from Seir," and the NRSV notes it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.plain: in Seir

readings.w: Septuagint, Syriac, Latin Vulgate; NRSV footnote
readings.plain: from Seir

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, since Seir is usually Edom, east of the Arabah, while Hormah is in the Negev. "From Seir" smooths the geography. "Seir" here may name hill country south of Judah, as in Joshua 15:10.

a: with his sons
p: The written Hebrew has "his son"; the scribes' reading has "his sons." Most versions follow the second.

readings.w: Qere (the reading marked by the Masoretes in the margin), Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint; KJV and most modern versions
readings.plain: with his sons

readings.w: Ketiv (the letters written in the Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: with his son

why: The Masoretes marked the plural to be read, and the ancient versions agree. The written form may be an old spelling of the same plural.

a: the voice of a god
t: A god, or the living God?
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint read "the voice of the living God," as in 5:26.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: the voice of God / a god
readings.plain: the voice of a god

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint, as generally cited
readings.orig: קול אלהים חיים / φωνὴν θεοῦ ζῶντος
readings.en: the voice of the living God
readings.plain: the voice of the living God

why: "Living" looks like an addition taken from the same idea in 5:26. The shorter Hebrew is more likely original, and it keeps the comparison with other nations' gods.

a: chose his descendants after him
p: The Hebrew says God chose "his descendants after him." The Samaritan and the ancient translations read "their... them," which many English versions print.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: and he chose his offspring after him
readings.plain: chose his descendants after him

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Syriac, Latin Vulgate; KJV, NRSV and ESV
readings.en: and he chose their offspring after them
readings.plain: chose their descendants after them

why: The singular is the harder reading after "your ancestors" (plural), and the versions look like a correction to make the grammar agree. "His" probably means Abraham's, the ancestor to whom the promise was first given, or each ancestor in turn. Compare 10:15, where the plural is used.

a: Mount Sion
p: The Hebrew has Sion, a name for Hermon found only here. The Syriac reads Sirion, as in 3:9, and the NRSV prints it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint
readings.plain: Mount Sion

readings.w: Syriac Peshitta; followed by the NRSV
readings.plain: Mount Sirion

why: Most witnesses have Sion, and it may be a genuine local name for the mountain. Sirion is the name 3:9 says the Sidonians used, and the Syriac may have harmonized with it, though the Hebrew could also be a copying slip for it.

a: my commands
p: The written Hebrew has "his commands"; the reading marked for the synagogue is "my commands," as in Exodus 20:6.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretes' reading), Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint; Exodus 20:6; KJV and modern versions
readings.plain: my commands

readings.w: Ketiv (the letters written in the Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: his commands

why: God is speaking in the first person ("those who love me"), and Exodus 20:6 has "my commands." The written "his" is probably a slip by a copyist, or a trace of Moses' own voice retelling God's words.

a: That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the day of the Sabbath.
t: A Qumran scroll adds the Exodus reason
p: 4QDeut-n adds the creation reason for the Sabbath from Exodus 20:11 after this verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint
readings.orig: עַל־כֵּן צִוְּךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
readings.en: therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day
readings.plain: That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the day of the Sabbath.

readings.w: Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-n (4Q41), late 1st century BC; the Nash Papyrus (about 150–100 BC) also mixes the Exodus and Deuteronomy forms
readings.orig: כי ששת ימים עשה יהוה את השמים ואת הארץ...
readings.en: adds: for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth...
readings.plain: That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the day of the Sabbath and set it apart as holy. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them, and on the seventh day he rested. That is why the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy.

why: All the main witnesses lack the addition. The scroll 4QDeut-n seems to have been a text for study or worship that brought the two forms of the Ten Words together, which shows how early readers felt the difference.
b: 4QDeut-n is a small scroll of selected passages, perhaps for personal use. Its addition shows that some Jews before Jesus wanted both reasons for the Sabbath, creation and the exodus, as the later Friday-night blessing over wine includes both.

a: You must not murder.
p: The Septuagint and the Nash Papyrus put adultery before murder. Goes with 5:18.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch, Dead Sea Scrolls of Deuteronomy
readings.plain: You must not murder.

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus), Nash Papyrus (about 150–100 BC), Philo; compare Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9
readings.plain: You must not commit adultery.

why: The Hebrew witnesses agree on the order murder, adultery, theft. The other order is old and widespread in Egypt and in Greek-speaking Judaism, and the New Testament sometimes follows it, but it is not the Hebrew text.
b: Philo of Alexandria explains the Greek order by saying adultery is the greatest of wrongs against a neighbor. Jesus' list in Mark 10:19 follows the Hebrew order, while Luke 18:20 and Romans 13:9 put adultery first.

a: And you must not commit adultery.
p: Goes with 5:17: in the Septuagint and the Nash Papyrus the second of these commands is murder.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch, Dead Sea Scrolls of Deuteronomy
readings.en: And you shall not commit adultery
readings.plain: And you must not commit adultery.

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus), Nash Papyrus, Philo
readings.plain: And you must not murder.

why: See 5:17. The Hebrew witnesses agree on the order.

a: or anything at all that belongs to your neighbor.
t: The Samaritan command about Mount Gerizim
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch adds a command to build an altar on Mount Gerizim, made of verses from 11:29–30 and 27:2–7.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Septuagint, Dead Sea Scrolls
readings.en: or anything that is your neighbor's
readings.plain: or anything at all that belongs to your neighbor.

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (here and in Exodus 20); manuscripts from the Middle Ages, text tradition older
readings.orig: והיה כי יביאך יהוה אלהיך אל ארץ הכנעני... והקמת לך אבנים גדלות... בהר גריזים
readings.en: adds: When the LORD your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites... set up great stones... on Mount Gerizim
readings.plain: or anything at all that belongs to your neighbor. When the LORD your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites that you are entering to take possession of, set up for yourself large stones, coat them with plaster, and write on them all the words of this law. When you have crossed the Jordan, set up these stones on Mount Gerizim, and build there an altar to the LORD your God. That mountain is on the other side of the Jordan, beyond the road to the west, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, across from Gilgal, beside the great tree of Moreh, across from Shechem.

why: No Jewish or Greek witness has the addition. It is built from other verses of Deuteronomy to make worship on Gerizim one of the Ten Words. The Samaritans count "I am the LORD your God" as a preface, so this becomes their tenth command.
b: The Samaritan Pentateuch also reads "Gerizim" for "Ebal" in 27:4. Many scholars now think "Gerizim" may be the older reading there, but the addition here is clearly a Samaritan expansion.

a: Listen, Israel:
p: The Septuagint and the Nash Papyrus put a heading before the Shema: "These are the rules and the rulings."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.plain: Listen, Israel:

readings.w: Septuagint; the Nash Papyrus (about 150–100 BC) has a similar line with "Moses commanded"
readings.orig: Καὶ ταῦτα τὰ δικαιώματα καὶ τὰ κρίματα... Ἄκουε, Ισραηλ
readings.en: And these are the statutes and the judgments that the Lord commanded the sons of Israel in the wilderness as they came out of the land of Egypt. Hear, O Israel
readings.plain: These are the rules and the rulings the LORD commanded the Israelites in the wilderness, when they came out of the land of Egypt. Listen, Israel:

why: The Hebrew witnesses lack the heading. It looks like a heading taken from 4:45 and 6:1, added where the Shema was copied or recited on its own after the Ten Words, as in the Nash Papyrus and in temple worship (Mishnah Tamid 5:1).

a: with all your heart
p: Some Septuagint manuscripts read "with all your mind." The Gospels give both heart and mind.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch, Dead Sea Scrolls; Septuagint Codex Alexandrinus ("heart")
readings.plain: with all your heart

readings.w: Septuagint Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD) and other Greek manuscripts
readings.plain: with all your mind

why: The Hebrew lev means both heart and mind; the Greek translators used either word. Following the Hebrew, this site says "heart."
b: The Gospels quote the Shema with four terms: heart, soul, mind and strength (Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27), or three (Matthew 22:37, heart, soul, mind). The extra word probably comes from the two Greek ways of rendering lev. The Septuagint also has "power" (dynamis) for me'od.

a: He is the one you must serve
p: The Greek adds "only" and "hold on to him." Jesus' answer in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8 quotes this Greek form.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.plain: He is the one you must serve

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Alexandrinus also reads "worship" for "fear"); quoted in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8
readings.orig: καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν κολληθήσῃ
readings.en: and him only you shall serve, and to him you shall cling
readings.plain: Him alone you must serve, and you must hold on to him

why: The Hebrew puts "him" first for emphasis, which the Greek spells out as "only." "Cling to him" comes from 10:20. The meaning is close, but the Gospel wording comes from the Greek.

a: commanded you
p: The Hebrew has "you." The Septuagint reads "us," as does the Jerusalem Talmud's version of the wise son's question.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch; the Passover Haggadah in common use
readings.plain: commanded you

readings.w: Septuagint; Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim 10:4) in its version of the wise son
readings.plain: commanded us

why: The Hebrew witnesses agree on "you"; the child asks about laws given to his parents' generation. "Us" smooths the question and may come from its use in the Passover service.

a: everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth
p: The Greek adds "word" and says "God" for "the LORD." Matthew 4:4 quotes the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: everything that comes out of the mouth of the LORD
readings.plain: everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth

readings.w: Septuagint; quoted in Matthew 4:4 (Luke 4:4 in the Byzantine text); KJV "every word"
readings.orig: παντὶ ῥήματι τῷ ἐκπορευομένῳ διὰ στόματος θεοῦ
readings.en: every word that goes out through the mouth of God
readings.plain: every word that comes out of the mouth of God

why: The Hebrew does not have "word"; the Greek supplied it to make the sense clear. The meaning is close, but the Hebrew can include whatever God decrees, such as the manna.

a: from the day I first knew you
t: I knew you, or he knew you?
p: The Septuagint reads "from the day he became known to you," making God, not Moses, the subject.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: from the day that I knew you
readings.plain: from the day I first knew you

readings.w: Septuagint, probably reading a Hebrew text with "his knowing" (da'to); the Samaritan Pentateuch is often cited with it
readings.orig: ἀπὸ τῆς ἡμέρας ἧς ἐγνώσθη ὑμῖν
readings.en: from the day he became known to you
readings.plain: from the day he made himself known to you

why: The Hebrew "I" fits Moses' speech: in his forty years with them, Israel has always rebelled. The Greek reading differs by one letter in Hebrew and may be a copying change.

a: The Israelites set out from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried.
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch rewrites verses 6–7 to match the route and Aaron's death at Mount Hor in Numbers 33.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Septuagint
readings.orig: וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נָסְעוּ מִבְּאֵרֹת בְּנֵי־יַעֲקָן מוֹסֵרָה
readings.en: The sons of Israel set out from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died
readings.plain: The Israelites set out from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried.

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (shortened here)
readings.orig: ובני ישראל נסעו ממסרות ויחנו בבני יעקן...
readings.en: The sons of Israel set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan... and camped at Mount Hor, and there Aaron died
readings.plain: The Israelites set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan. From there they set out and camped at Hor-haggidgad... and from there they set out and camped at Mount Hor. There Aaron died, and there he was buried.

why: The Samaritan text, like other harmonizing texts, makes Deuteronomy agree with Numbers 33:31–38. The Masoretic reading is the harder one and is more likely to be original.

a: then I will give your land its rain
t: I will give, or he will give?
p: The Hebrew has God speak: "I will give." The Samaritan and Greek keep Moses speaking: "he will give." Goes with 11:15.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; KJV and most versions
readings.plain: then I will give your land its rain

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Latin Vulgate; followed by the NRSV
readings.plain: then he will give your land its rain

why: The Hebrew shift into God's own voice is the harder reading: Moses quotes God, as in 7:4 and 11:13 ("my commands"). Scribes and translators made it smoother. The Shema recited in the synagogue keeps "I will give."

a: I will give grass in your fields
t: I will give, or he will give?
p: Goes with 11:14: the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint read "he will give."

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.plain: I will give grass in your fields

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint
readings.plain: He will give grass in your fields

a: beside the great trees of Moreh
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch reads "beside the great tree of Moreh, across from Shechem," tying the mountains to the Samaritan holy place.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.plain: beside the great trees of Moreh

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch; the Septuagint also has the singular "tree"
readings.en: beside the oak of Moreh, across from Shechem
readings.plain: beside the great tree of Moreh, across from Shechem

why: "Across from Shechem" is a clarifying addition that suits the Samaritan claim for Mount Gerizim. It is geographically correct (see Genesis 12:6), but it is not in the other witnesses.
